cards.front: What is a proposition?
cards.back: A declarative sentence that is either true or false.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

fields.Front: What is a proposition?
fields.Back: A declarative sentence that is either true or false.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

cards.front: Why is "\(x + 1 = 3\)" not a proposition?
cards.back: Its truth depends on \(x\); it becomes one once \(x\) is fixed or quantified.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

fields.Front: Why is "\(x + 1 = 3\)" not a proposition?
fields.Back: Its truth depends on \(x\); it becomes one once \(x\) is fixed or quantified.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

cards.front: Is a sentence whose truth nobody knows yet (e.g. Goldbach's conjecture) a proposition?
cards.back: Yes: it only needs a definite truth value, not a known one.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

fields.Front: Is a sentence whose truth nobody knows yet (e.g. Goldbach's conjecture) a proposition?
fields.Back: Yes: it only needs a definite truth value, not a known one.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Propositions

cards.front: When is the conjunction \(A \wedge B\) true?
cards.back: Only when both \(A\) and \(B\) are true.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

fields.Front: When is the conjunction \(A \wedge B\) true?
fields.Back: Only when both \(A\) and \(B\) are true.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

cards.front: When is the disjunction \(A \vee B\) true?
cards.back: When at least one of \(A\), \(B\) is true (also when both are).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

fields.Front: When is the disjunction \(A \vee B\) true?
fields.Back: When at least one of \(A\), \(B\) is true (also when both are).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

cards.front: What does the negation \(\neg A\) do?
cards.back: It reverses the truth value of \(A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

fields.Front: What does the negation \(\neg A\) do?
fields.Back: It reverses the truth value of \(A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

cards.front: When is the exclusive or \(A \oplus B\) true?
cards.back: Exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have different truth values.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

fields.Front: When is the exclusive or \(A \oplus B\) true?
fields.Back: Exactly when \(A\) and \(B\) have different truth values.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Constructing propositions

cards.front: Is mathematical "or" (\(\vee\)) inclusive or exclusive?
cards.back: Inclusive: \(A \vee B\) is true when both are true.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Basic connectives

fields.Front: Is mathematical "or" (\(\vee\)) inclusive or exclusive?
fields.Back: Inclusive: \(A \vee B\) is true when both are true.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Basic connectives

cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Truth tables

fields.Front: How many rows does a truth table with \(n\) propositions have?
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Truth tables

cards.front: When is the implication \(A \Rightarrow B\) false?
cards.back: Only when \(A\) is true and \(B\) is false.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication: A implies B

fields.Front: When is the implication \(A \Rightarrow B\) false?
fields.Back: Only when \(A\) is true and \(B\) is false.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication: A implies B

cards.front: In \(A \Rightarrow B\), what are \(A\) and \(B\) called?
cards.back: \(A\) is the hypothesis, \(B\) the conclusion.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication: A implies B

fields.Front: In \(A \Rightarrow B\), what are \(A\) and \(B\) called?
fields.Back: \(A\) is the hypothesis, \(B\) the conclusion.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication: A implies B

cards.front: What is the truth value of \(A \Rightarrow B\) when \(A\) is false?
cards.back: True, whatever \(B\) is.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication when the hypothesis is false

fields.Front: What is the truth value of \(A \Rightarrow B\) when \(A\) is false?
fields.Back: True, whatever \(B\) is.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication when the hypothesis is false

cards.front: What must a counterexample to \(A \Rightarrow B\) satisfy?
cards.back: \(A\) true and \(B\) false.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication when the hypothesis is false

fields.Front: What must a counterexample to \(A \Rightarrow B\) satisfy?
fields.Back: \(A\) true and \(B\) false.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication when the hypothesis is false

cards.front: When is \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) true?
cards.back: When \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

fields.Front: When is \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) true?
fields.Back: When \(A\) and \(B\) have the same truth value.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

cards.front: Write \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) with two implications.
cards.back: \((A \Rightarrow B) \wedge (B \Rightarrow A)\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

fields.Front: Write \(A \Leftrightarrow B\) with two implications.
fields.Back: \((A \Rightarrow B) \wedge (B \Rightarrow A)\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

cards.front: How do you prove an "if and only if" statement?
cards.back: Prove both directions: \(A \Rightarrow B\) and \(B \Rightarrow A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

fields.Front: How do you prove an "if and only if" statement?
fields.Back: Prove both directions: \(A \Rightarrow B\) and \(B \Rightarrow A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › If and only if

cards.front: In \(A \Rightarrow B\), which is sufficient and which is necessary?
cards.back: \(A\) is sufficient for \(B\); \(B\) is necessary for \(A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Necessary and sufficient

fields.Front: In \(A \Rightarrow B\), which is sufficient and which is necessary?
fields.Back: \(A\) is sufficient for \(B\); \(B\) is necessary for \(A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Necessary and sufficient

cards.front: Differentiable ⇒ continuous. Which property is necessary and which sufficient?
cards.back: Differentiability is sufficient; continuity is necessary.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Necessary and sufficient

fields.Front: Differentiable ⇒ continuous. Which property is necessary and which sufficient?
fields.Back: Differentiability is sufficient; continuity is necessary.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Necessary and sufficient

cards.front: Which implication does "\(A\) only if \(B\)" mean?
cards.back:
\(A \Rightarrow B\) (not \(B \Rightarrow A\)).
After "if" comes the hypothesis; after "only if" the conclusion.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication in words

fields.Front: Which implication does "\(A\) only if \(B\)" mean?
fields.Back:
\(A \Rightarrow B\) (not \(B \Rightarrow A\)).
After "if" comes the hypothesis; after "only if" the conclusion.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication in words

cards.front: Which implication does "\(B\) if \(A\)" mean?
cards.back: \(A \Rightarrow B\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication in words

fields.Front: Which implication does "\(B\) if \(A\)" mean?
fields.Back: \(A \Rightarrow B\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Implication in words

cards.front: What is the converse of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
cards.back: \(B \Rightarrow A\); not equivalent in general.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

fields.Front: What is the converse of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: \(B \Rightarrow A\); not equivalent in general.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

cards.front: What is the inverse of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
cards.back: \(\neg A \Rightarrow \neg B\); not equivalent in general.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

fields.Front: What is the inverse of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: \(\neg A \Rightarrow \neg B\); not equivalent in general.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

cards.front: What is the contrapositive of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
cards.back: \(\neg B \Rightarrow \neg A\), which is equivalent to \(A \Rightarrow B\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

fields.Front: What is the contrapositive of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: \(\neg B \Rightarrow \neg A\), which is equivalent to \(A \Rightarrow B\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

cards.front: "If \(x > 2\), then \(x^2 > 4\)" is true. Give a counterexample to its converse.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

fields.Front: "If \(x > 2\), then \(x^2 > 4\)" is true. Give a counterexample to its converse.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Converse, inverse, contrapositive

cards.front: Give the precedence of \(\neg, \wedge, \vee, \Rightarrow, \Leftrightarrow\), strongest first.
cards.back: \(\neg\), then \(\wedge\), \(\vee\), \(\Rightarrow\), \(\Leftrightarrow\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

fields.Front: Give the precedence of \(\neg, \wedge, \vee, \Rightarrow, \Leftrightarrow\), strongest first.
fields.Back: \(\neg\), then \(\wedge\), \(\vee\), \(\Rightarrow\), \(\Leftrightarrow\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

cards.front: How is \(\neg A \wedge B\) read?
cards.back: \((\neg A) \wedge B\), not \(\neg(A \wedge B)\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

fields.Front: How is \(\neg A \wedge B\) read?
fields.Back: \((\neg A) \wedge B\), not \(\neg(A \wedge B)\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

cards.front: When may parentheses be left out between operations?
cards.back: With repeated identical operations (associativity), e.g. \(A \vee B \vee C\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

fields.Front: When may parentheses be left out between operations?
fields.Back: With repeated identical operations (associativity), e.g. \(A \vee B \vee C\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Precedence rules

cards.front: What is a tautology? Give an example.
cards.back: A statement that is always true, e.g. \(A \vee \neg A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

fields.Front: What is a tautology? Give an example.
fields.Back: A statement that is always true, e.g. \(A \vee \neg A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

cards.front: What is a contradiction (in logic)? Give an example.
cards.back: A statement that is always false, e.g. \(A \wedge \neg A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

fields.Front: What is a contradiction (in logic)? Give an example.
fields.Back: A statement that is always false, e.g. \(A \wedge \neg A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

cards.front: When are two statements \(P\) and \(Q\) logically equivalent?
cards.back: When they have the same truth value for every assignment.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

fields.Front: When are two statements \(P\) and \(Q\) logically equivalent?
fields.Back: When they have the same truth value for every assignment.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

cards.front: How can you prove a logical equivalence?
cards.back: Build truth tables and check that the final columns agree.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

fields.Front: How can you prove a logical equivalence?
fields.Back: Build truth tables and check that the final columns agree.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Tautology, contradiction, equivalence

cards.front: State the idempotent laws of logic.
cards.back: \(A \wedge A \Leftrightarrow A\) and \(A \vee A \Leftrightarrow A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

fields.Front: State the idempotent laws of logic.
fields.Back: \(A \wedge A \Leftrightarrow A\) and \(A \vee A \Leftrightarrow A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

cards.front: State the commutative laws of logic.
cards.back: \(A \wedge B \Leftrightarrow B \wedge A\) and \(A \vee B \Leftrightarrow B \vee A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

fields.Front: State the commutative laws of logic.
fields.Back: \(A \wedge B \Leftrightarrow B \wedge A\) and \(A \vee B \Leftrightarrow B \vee A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

cards.front: State the associative law for \(\wedge\).
cards.back: \(A \wedge (B \wedge C) \Leftrightarrow (A \wedge B) \wedge C\); the same for \(\vee\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

fields.Front: State the associative law for \(\wedge\).
fields.Back: \(A \wedge (B \wedge C) \Leftrightarrow (A \wedge B) \wedge C\); the same for \(\vee\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

cards.front: State the law of double negation.
cards.back: \(\neg\neg A \Leftrightarrow A\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

fields.Front: State the law of double negation.
fields.Back: \(\neg\neg A \Leftrightarrow A\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Laws of propositional logic

cards.front: Expand \(A \wedge (B \vee C)\) with the distributive law.
cards.back: \((A \wedge B) \vee (A \wedge C)\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

fields.Front: Expand \(A \wedge (B \vee C)\) with the distributive law.
fields.Back: \((A \wedge B) \vee (A \wedge C)\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

cards.front: Expand \(A \vee (B \wedge C)\) with the distributive law.
cards.back: \((A \vee B) \wedge (A \vee C)\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

fields.Front: Expand \(A \vee (B \wedge C)\) with the distributive law.
fields.Back: \((A \vee B) \wedge (A \vee C)\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

cards.front: De Morgan: what is \(\neg(A \wedge B)\)?
cards.back: \(\neg A \vee \neg B\): at least one fails.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

fields.Front: De Morgan: what is \(\neg(A \wedge B)\)?
fields.Back: \(\neg A \vee \neg B\): at least one fails.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

cards.front: De Morgan: what is \(\neg(A \vee B)\)?
cards.back: \(\neg A \wedge \neg B\): both fail.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

fields.Front: De Morgan: what is \(\neg(A \vee B)\)?
fields.Back: \(\neg A \wedge \neg B\): both fail.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Distributive and De Morgan's laws

cards.front: Negate "\(n\) is positive and odd" for an integer \(n\).
cards.back:
\(n \le 0\) or \(n\) is even.
"Negative" would forget \(n = 0\).

fields.Front: Negate "\(n\) is positive and odd" for an integer \(n\).
fields.Back:
\(n \le 0\) or \(n\) is even.
"Negative" would forget \(n = 0\).

cards.front: What is the negation of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
cards.back: \(A \wedge \neg B\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating an implication

fields.Front: What is the negation of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: \(A \wedge \neg B\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating an implication

cards.front: Why isn't "\(A \Rightarrow \neg B\)" the negation of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
cards.back: Both are true when \(A\) is false; a negation must be true exactly when the original is false.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating an implication

fields.Front: Why isn't "\(A \Rightarrow \neg B\)" the negation of \(A \Rightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: Both are true when \(A\) is false; a negation must be true exactly when the original is false.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating an implication

cards.front: What is the negation of \(A \Leftrightarrow B\)?
cards.back: \((A \wedge \neg B) \vee (\neg A \wedge B)\): exactly one is true.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating "if and only if"

fields.Front: What is the negation of \(A \Leftrightarrow B\)?
fields.Back: \((A \wedge \neg B) \vee (\neg A \wedge B)\): exactly one is true.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Negating "if and only if"

cards.front: What is a predicate?
cards.back: A statement with variables; it becomes a proposition once they are fixed or quantified.

cards.front: What do \(\forall a\, P(a)\) and \(\exists a\, P(a)\) say?
cards.back: \(\forall\): \(P(a)\) holds for every \(a\); \(\exists\): it holds for at least one \(a\).

fields.Front: What do \(\forall a\, P(a)\) and \(\exists a\, P(a)\) say?
fields.Back: \(\forall\): \(P(a)\) holds for every \(a\); \(\exists\): it holds for at least one \(a\).

cards.front: On a finite domain \(\{a_1, a_2, a_3\}\), what are \(\forall a\, P(a)\) and \(\exists a\, P(a)\)?
cards.back: A big AND \(P(a_1) \wedge P(a_2) \wedge P(a_3)\) and a big OR.
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Quantified statements

fields.Front: On a finite domain \(\{a_1, a_2, a_3\}\), what are \(\forall a\, P(a)\) and \(\exists a\, P(a)\)?
fields.Back: A big AND \(P(a_1) \wedge P(a_2) \wedge P(a_3)\) and a big OR.
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Quantified statements

cards.front: How do you prove and how do you disprove \(\forall x \in D: P(x)\)?

cards.front: How do you prove and how do you disprove \(\exists x \in D: P(x)\)?

cards.front: What is a proof?
cards.back: A chain of valid implications from accepted assumptions to the conclusion.

fields.Back: A chain of valid implications from accepted assumptions to the conclusion.

cards.front: How does a proof of \(P \Rightarrow Q\) by contradiction work?

cards.front: Prove there is no largest integer: what is the contradiction?

fields.Front: Prove there is no largest integer: what is the contradiction?

fields.Back: When the statement is indexed by \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
fields.Source: 1 Elements of Logic › Choosing a proof method

cards.front: Why don't examples prove a "for all" statement?
cards.back:
They only cover some cases; a proof must cover every case.
\(n^2 - n + 41\) is prime for \(n = 1, \ldots, 40\), not for \(n = 41\).
cards.source: 1 Elements of Logic › Common proof mistakes

cards.front: Why is \(\{1\} \in \{1, 2\}\) false, although \(\{1\} \subseteq \{1, 2\}\) is true?
cards.back:
The elements of \(\{1, 2\}\) are the numbers 1 and 2, not the set \(\{1\}\).
Left of \(\in\) stands an element; on both sides of \(\subseteq\) stand sets.

fields.Back: \(\bar z = x - yi\).
fields.Source: 4 Complex Numbers › Conjugate and modulus

cards.front: Define the modulus \(\lvert z \rvert\) of \(z = x + yi\).
cards.back: \(\lvert z \rvert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\).
cards.source: 4 Complex Numbers › Conjugate and modulus

fields.Front: Define the modulus \(\lvert z \rvert\) of \(z = x + yi\).
fields.Back: \(\lvert z \rvert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\).

cards.front: What do \(\bar z\) and \(\lvert z \rvert\) mean geometrically?
cards.back: \(\bar z\): reflection across the real axis; \(\lvert z \rvert\): distance from \(z\) to 0.
cards.source: 4 Complex Numbers › Conjugate and modulus

cards.front: What is \(z \bar z\)?
cards.back: \(\lvert z \rvert^2\), always a real number.

cards.front: How does conjugation act on \(z_1 + z_2\) and on \(z_1 z_2\)?
cards.back: \(\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar z_1 + \bar z_2\) and \(\overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar z_1\,\bar z_2\).

fields.Front: How does conjugation act on \(z_1 + z_2\) and on \(z_1 z_2\)?

cards.front: Express \(\operatorname{Re} z\) using \(z\) and \(\bar z\).
cards.back: \(\operatorname{Re} z = \frac{z + \bar z}{2}\).
cards.source: 4 Complex Numbers › Useful conjugate identities

fields.Front: Express \(\operatorname{Re} z\) using \(z\) and \(\bar z\).
fields.Back: \(\operatorname{Re} z = \frac{z + \bar z}{2}\).
fields.Source: 4 Complex Numbers › Useful conjugate identities

cards.front: Express \(\operatorname{Im} z\) using \(z\) and \(\bar z\).
cards.back: \(\operatorname{Im} z = \frac{z - \bar z}{2i}\).
cards.source: 4 Complex Numbers › Useful conjugate identities

fields.Front: Express \(\operatorname{Im} z\) using \(z\) and \(\bar z\).
fields.Back: \(\operatorname{Im} z = \frac{z - \bar z}{2i}\).
fields.Source: 4 Complex Numbers › Useful conjugate identities

cards.front: What is \(\lvert z_1 z_2 \rvert\)?
cards.back: \(\lvert z_1 \rvert\,\lvert z_2 \rvert\).

cards.front: Why is \(\lvert z \rvert^2 \neq z^2\) for complex \(z\)? Use \(z = 1 + i\).
cards.back: \(z^2 = 2i\), but \(\lvert z \rvert^2 = z \bar z = 2\).
cards.source: 4 Complex Numbers › Useful conjugate identities

cards.front: Give \(\frac{1}{z}\) for \(z \neq 0\) using the conjugate.
cards.back: \(\frac{1}{z} = \frac{\bar z}{\lvert z \rvert^2}\).

fields.Front: Give \(\frac{1}{z}\) for \(z \neq 0\) using the conjugate.

cards.front: How do you compute \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\) in Cartesian form?
cards.back: Multiply top and bottom by \(\bar z_2\); the denominator becomes the real \(\lvert z_2 \rvert^2\).

fields.Front: How do you compute \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}\) in Cartesian form?

cards.back: \(z = r(\cos\varphi + i\sin\varphi)\), with \(x = r\cos\varphi\), \(y = r\sin\varphi\).

cards.front: Converting \(z = x + yi\) to polar form: how do you get the right angle?
cards.back:
Sketch the point; use \(\cos\varphi = x/r\), \(\sin\varphi = y/r\) to fix the quadrant.
\(\tan\varphi = y/x\) alone can't tell \(1 + i\) from \(-1 - i\).

cards.front: State De Moivre's formula.
cards.back: \((re^{i\varphi})^n = r^n e^{in\varphi}\), i.e. \(r^n(\cos n\varphi + i\sin n\varphi)\).

cards.front: How do you compute a high power like \((\sqrt3 + i)^6\) quickly?
cards.back:
Convert to polar form, apply De Moivre, convert back.
\((2e^{i\pi/6})^6 = 64 e^{i\pi} = -64\).

cards.front: Define the graph \(\Gamma(f)\) of a function \(f\).

cards.front: When is \(f : X \to Y\) injective?

fields.Back: As \(\inf\) and \(\sup\) of the set of values \(\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}\).
fields.Source: 6 Sequences › Infimum and supremum

cards.front: What are \(\inf_n \frac1n\) and \(\sup_n \frac1n\)?
cards.back: \(\inf = 0\) (not a term) and \(\sup = 1 = a_1\).
cards.source: 6 Sequences › Infimum and supremum

fields.Front: What are \(\inf_n \frac1n\) and \(\sup_n \frac1n\)?
fields.Back: \(\inf = 0\) (not a term) and \(\sup = 1 = a_1\).
fields.Source: 6 Sequences › Infimum and supremum

cards.front: Which two conditions make the real number \(m\) equal to \(\inf_n a_n\)?
cards.back: \(a_n \ge m\) for all \(n\), and \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n : a_n < m + \varepsilon\).
cards.source: 6 Sequences › Characterising the infimum and supremum

fields.Front: Which two conditions make the real number \(m\) equal to \(\inf_n a_n\)?
fields.Back: \(a_n \ge m\) for all \(n\), and \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n : a_n < m + \varepsilon\).
fields.Source: 6 Sequences › Characterising the infimum and supremum

cards.front: Which two conditions make the real number \(M\) equal to \(\sup_n a_n\)?
cards.back: \(a_n \le M\) for all \(n\), and \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n : a_n > M - \varepsilon\).
cards.source: 6 Sequences › Characterising the infimum and supremum

fields.Front: Which two conditions make the real number \(M\) equal to \(\sup_n a_n\)?
fields.Back: \(a_n \le M\) for all \(n\), and \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n : a_n > M - \varepsilon\).
fields.Source: 6 Sequences › Characterising the infimum and supremum

cards.front: When is a sequence non-decreasing?
cards.back: \(a_{n+1} \ge a_n\) for all \(n\).

cards.front: When is a sequence called monotonic?
cards.back: When it is non-decreasing or non-increasing.

fields.Front: When is a sequence called monotonic?
fields.Back: When it is non-decreasing or non-increasing.

cards.front: How do you test a sequence for monotonicity with the difference test?
cards.back: Find the sign of \(a_{n+1} - a_n\) for all \(n\).

fields.Front: How do you test a sequence for monotonicity with the difference test?
fields.Back: Find the sign of \(a_{n+1} - a_n\) for all \(n\).

cards.front: When can you use the ratio test for monotonicity, and how?
cards.back: For positive terms: compare \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\) with 1.

fields.Front: When can you use the ratio test for monotonicity, and how?
fields.Back: For positive terms: compare \(\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\) with 1.

cards.front: Why is comparing neighbours enough to prove a sequence monotonic?
cards.back: Any \(a_i \le a_j\) with \(i < j\) follows by chaining the steps in between.

fields.Front: Why is comparing neighbours enough to prove a sequence monotonic?
fields.Back: Any \(a_i \le a_j\) with \(i < j\) follows by chaining the steps in between.

cards.front: How do you show a sequence is not monotonic?
cards.back:
Give one step up and one step down.
\((-1)^n\) goes up from \(a_1\) to \(a_2\) and down to \(a_3\).

fields.Front: How do you show a sequence is not monotonic?

cards.front: Which monotonicity properties does a constant sequence have?
cards.back: Non-decreasing and non-increasing, but not strictly monotonic.

cards.front: Give \(\inf\) and \(\sup\) of \(a_n = \frac{n}{n + 1}\).

cards.front: What part of a recursive sequence's definition can change all its properties?
cards.back:
The initial value.
\(a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n^2 + 1}{2}\): \(a_1 = 1\) constant, \(\frac12\) bounded, \(2\) unbounded.
cards.source: 6 Sequences › A recurrence with different initial values

fields.Front: What part of a recursive sequence's definition can change all its properties?
fields.Back:
The initial value.
\(a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n^2 + 1}{2}\): \(a_1 = 1\) constant, \(\frac12\) bounded, \(2\) unbounded.

cards.back: \(\frac{(a_n - 1)^2}{2} \ge 0\), so the sequence never decreases.

cards.front: What is a fixed point of a recursion \(a_{n+1} = g(a_n)\)?
cards.back: A value \(x\) with \(g(x) = x\); starting there gives a constant sequence.

cards.front: How do you show a recursive sequence stays in an interval like \((0, 1)\)?
cards.back: By induction: \(a_1\) is in it, and \(a_n\) in it implies \(a_{n+1}\) in it.

fields.Front: How do you show a recursive sequence stays in an interval like \((0, 1)\)?

cards.front: Which sequence approaches Euler's number \(e\), and how does it behave?

fields.Front: Which sequence approaches Euler's number \(e\), and how does it behave?

After the peak, check how low the tail goes for the infimum.

cards.front: Give the explicit formula for \(u_{n+1} = q\,u_n + c\) (\(q \ne 1\)).
cards.back: \(u_n = L + (u_1 - L)q^{n-1}\) with fixed point \(L = \frac{c}{1 - q}\).

cards.front: Give the explicit formula for \(u_{n+1} = u_n + h(n)\).

cards.front: State the squeeze theorem.

cards.front: How do you find a limit like \(\frac{\cos n}{n}\), with a bounded factor that has no limit?

cards.front: How do you show a recursive sequence is Cauchy without its limit?
cards.back:
Show \(\lvert a_{n+1} - a_n \rvert \le q\lvert a_n - a_{n-1} \rvert\) with \(q < 1\).
Then the differences shrink geometrically.

fields.Front: How do you show a recursive sequence is Cauchy without its limit?

cards.front: State the Cauchy criterion for a series.

Every late block of terms has a small sum, however long.

cards.front: State the ratio test with \(L = \lim \left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert\).

fields.Front: State the ratio test with \(L = \lim \left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert\).

cards.front: Ratio test without a limit: what is needed for absolute convergence?
cards.back:
One fixed \(L < 1\) with \(\left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert \le L\) for all late \(n\).
Each ratio being \(< 1\) is not enough.

fields.Front: Ratio test without a limit: what is needed for absolute convergence?

cards.front: Why does \(\left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert \ge 1\) for all late \(n\) imply divergence?

fields.Front: Why does \(\left\lvert \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right\rvert \ge 1\) for all late \(n\) imply divergence?

cards.front: State Dirichlet's test for \(\sum a_n b_n\).
cards.back: \(a_n \ge 0\) non-increasing with \(a_n \to 0\), and the partial sums of \(b_n\) bounded ⇒ converges.

fields.Front: State Dirichlet's test for \(\sum a_n b_n\).

cards.front: Why does \(\sum \frac{\sin(n\alpha)}{n}\) converge for every \(\alpha\)?
cards.back: Dirichlet: \(\frac1n \downarrow 0\) and \(\sum_{j \le N} \sin(j\alpha)\) is bounded.

fields.Front: Why does \(\sum \frac{\sin(n\alpha)}{n}\) converge for every \(\alpha\)?

cards.front: State Abel's test for \(\sum a_n b_n\).

cards.front: Define \(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = a\) with \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\).
